items.stem: What is the balance of payments?
options: A record of the government’s income and spending
The total debt owed by a country
A record of all financial transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world over a period
The difference between exports and imports of goods only
items.answer: A record of all financial transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world over a period
items.markingKey: Current account, capital account and financial account.

items.stem: Explain the difference between primary income and secondary income in the current account.
items.answer: Primary income is income earned from factors of production abroad: wages, profits, interest and dividends. Secondary income is current transfers with nothing given in return, such as remittances and foreign aid.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: primary = factor income with example; 1 mark: secondary = transfers with example [2]

items.stem: Explain why the export of a service is recorded as a credit in the current account.
items.answer: Foreign residents pay for the service, so money flows into the country, adding to its earnings from abroad.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: payment from abroad; 1 mark: inflow = credit [2]

items.stem: Migrants from Sundara living permanently in Calvania send money home to their families. Where, and on which side, is this transaction recorded in the current account of Sundara?
items.answer: Secondary income (credit)
items.markingKey: Secondary income (credit): remittances are current transfers into Sundara.

items.stem: The government of Istrana gives foreign aid to Merania. Where, and on which side, is this transaction recorded in the current account of Istrana? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Secondary income (debit): a current transfer abroad with nothing received in return.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Secondary income (debit); 1 mark: explanation – a current transfer abroad with nothing received in return. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Valdoria’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 210, imports of goods 260, exports of services 95, imports of services 40, primary income balance −8, secondary income balance 15. GDP is $1200bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Identify which component of the current account includes remittances. (b) Explain why the primary income balance is negative.
items.answer: (a) Secondary income (current transfers). (b) Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Secondary income (current transfers). [1] (b) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2]

items.stem: Which is included in primary income in the current account?
options: Profits and interest received on investments abroad
Purchase of shares in a foreign company
items.answer: Profits and interest received on investments abroad
items.markingKey: Investment income and compensation of employees.

items.stem: Explain the four components of the current account.
items.answer: Trade in goods (exports and imports of physical goods); trade in services (tourism, transport, finance); primary income (wages, profits, interest, dividends); secondary income (transfers such as remittances and aid).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each component explained [4]

items.stem: The table shows data for Tarvia’s current account in one year. Exports of goods $230bn; imports of goods $110bn; exports of services $50bn; imports of services $55bn; primary income balance −$8bn; secondary income balance −$3bn. What is the current account balance?

Identify where each transaction is recorded in the current account of Pelora, and whether it is a credit or a debit. (i) Households in Pelora buy bottled water made in Jovania. (ii) Tourists from Jovania spend their holidays in Auckland, Pelora.
items.answer: (i) Trade in goods (debit) (ii) Trade in services (credit)
items.markingKey: (i) Trade in goods (debit) – import of goods means money leaves Pelora. [2] (ii) Trade in services (credit) – spending by foreign tourists is an export of services. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: The currency of Selmaria has appreciated strongly over the past two years. Explain the components of the current account of the balance of payments.
items.answer: Trade in goods, trade in services, primary income, secondary income; credits and debits with examples; distinction from the financial account.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Trade in goods, trade in services, primary income, secondary income; credits and debits with examples; distinction from the financial account. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Which is most likely to cause a current account deficit?
options: Rapid growth in the incomes of trading partners
A recession in the domestic economy
Rapid growth in domestic incomes increasing demand for imports
items.answer: Rapid growth in domestic incomes increasing demand for imports
items.markingKey: Cyclical deficit.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a cyclical and a structural current account deficit.
items.answer: A cyclical deficit results from high demand in a boom (imports rise with income) and falls in a downturn; a structural deficit reflects long-term weaknesses such as low productivity or poor quality and persists through the cycle.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: cyclical linked to cycle/demand; 1 mark: structural long-term competitiveness [2]

items.stem: Explain how relatively high inflation can cause a current account deficit.
items.answer: If domestic prices rise faster than abroad, exports become less price competitive and imports relatively cheaper, so exports fall and imports rise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: loss of price competitiveness; 1 mark: exports fall/imports rise [2]

items.stem: Firms in Loristan have lower productivity than foreign rivals and lose export markets. Which cause of a current account imbalance is described?
items.answer: Structural cause (lack of competitiveness)
items.markingKey: Structural cause (lack of competitiveness): long-term weakness in non-price and price competitiveness.

items.stem: The world price of oil, Valdoria’s main export, rises sharply. Which cause of a current account imbalance is described? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Rising world prices of exports: export revenue rises if demand is price inelastic, causing a surplus.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Rising world prices of exports; 1 mark: explanation – export revenue rises if demand is price inelastic, causing a surplus. [2]

items.stem: For each case, identify the cause of the change in the current account and explain it. (i) Incomes in Merania grow rapidly during a boom and households buy many more imported goods. (ii) Households in Merania save a large share of income and spend little on imports.
items.answer: (i) Cyclical cause (high domestic demand) (ii) High domestic saving (low demand)
items.markingKey: (i) Cyclical cause (high domestic demand) – rising income raises imports through the marginal propensity to import. [2] (ii) High domestic saving (low demand) – low consumption keeps imports down, contributing to a surplus. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: Jovania’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 210, imports of goods 290, exports of services 60, imports of services 50, primary income balance −12, secondary income balance 10. GDP is $1200bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Calculate the current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP. (b) Explain why the primary income balance is negative.
items.answer: (a) −$72bn; −6% of GDP. (b) Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: −$72bn; −6% of GDP. [2] (b) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Westaria’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 240, imports of goods 260, exports of services 95, imports of services 50, primary income balance −12, secondary income balance 10. GDP is $800bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Identify which component of the current account includes remittances. (b) Explain two possible causes of the deficit on trade in goods.
items.answer: (a) Secondary income (current transfers). (b) Strong credit-fuelled consumer demand raises imports (cyclical); the 8% appreciation makes exports dearer and imports cheaper.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Secondary income (current transfers). [1] (b) Credit: Strong credit-fuelled consumer demand raises imports (cyclical); the 8% appreciation makes exports dearer and imports cheaper. [4]

items.stem: What is meant by a structural current account deficit?
options: A deficit that occurs only during a boom
A deficit caused by long-term weaknesses such as low productivity or poor product quality
A deficit caused by a single bad harvest
A deficit on the financial account
items.answer: A deficit caused by long-term weaknesses such as low productivity or poor product quality
items.markingKey: Persists through the cycle.

items.stem: Explain two causes of a current account surplus.
items.answer: Competitive exports (productivity, quality); high world prices for its commodity exports; high saving/low domestic demand; undervalued currency; large investment income from abroad.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two causes, 1 mark each for explanation [4]

items.stem: Lina makes the following statement: ‘An appreciation of Lunaria’s currency will increase its exports.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: Appreciation raises the foreign-currency price of exports, so export volumes tend to fall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Appreciation raises the foreign-currency price of exports, so export volumes tend to fall. [2]

items.stem: The currency of Selmaria appreciates by 15% against its trading partners. Which cause of a current account imbalance is described?
items.answer: Exchange rate appreciation
items.markingKey: Exchange rate appreciation: exports become dearer abroad and imports cheaper.

items.stem: Kestria has had a current account deficit of over 5% of GDP for several years. Explain the possible causes of a current account deficit.
items.answer: Cyclical (high growth, mpm), structural (productivity, quality, narrow export base), exchange rate appreciation, relative inflation, weak foreign demand, falling export prices.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Cyclical (high growth, mpm), structural (productivity, quality, narrow export base), exchange rate appreciation, relative inflation, weak foreign demand, falling export prices. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Marvona has had a current account deficit of over 5% of GDP for several years. Assess whether a current account deficit is mainly caused by a lack of international competitiveness.
items.answer: For: Structural weaknesses explain persistent deficits; low productivity and high unit labour costs. Against: Cyclical demand, exchange rates and foreign recessions also matter; investment-led deficits; depends on the country and period; judgement. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Structural weaknesses explain persistent deficits; low productivity and high unit labour costs. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Cyclical demand, exchange rates and foreign recessions also matter; investment-led deficits; depends on the country and period; judgement. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]

items.stem: Which is a likely consequence of a large and persistent current account deficit?
options: Upward pressure on the exchange rate
A rise in foreign currency reserves
Downward pressure on the exchange rate
items.answer: Downward pressure on the exchange rate
items.markingKey: Supply of currency exceeds demand.

items.stem: Explain why a current account deficit financed by short-term borrowing may be a problem.
items.answer: Short-term capital ("hot money") can leave quickly if confidence falls, causing a sharp depreciation; debt and interest payments build up.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: capital can leave quickly/currency crisis; 1 mark: rising debt/interest [2]

items.stem: Explain two possible consequences of a large current account surplus for an economy.
items.answer: Appreciation reduces future competitiveness; inflationary pressure from high net exports; accumulation of reserves; criticism or retaliation from partners; it may mean domestic consumption is low.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two consequences, 1 mark each for explanation [4]

items.stem: A persistent deficit leads to a fall in demand for Merania’s currency. Which consequence of a current account imbalance is described?
options: Pressure for appreciation and international tension
items.answer: Pressure for depreciation
items.markingKey: Pressure for depreciation: more currency is supplied to buy imports than is demanded for exports.

items.stem: Nordavia sells foreign currency reserves to support its exchange rate while in deficit. Which consequence of a current account imbalance is described? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Loss of foreign currency reserves: reserves are used to finance the deficit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Loss of foreign currency reserves; 1 mark: explanation – reserves are used to finance the deficit. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Tarvia’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 210, imports of goods 290, exports of services 95, imports of services 40, primary income balance −12, secondary income balance 10. GDP is $1000bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Calculate the current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP. (b) Explain why the primary income balance is negative.
items.answer: (a) −$27bn; −2.7% of GDP. (b) Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: −$27bn; −2.7% of GDP. [2] (b) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a current account deficit is not necessarily a problem.
items.answer: It may be small and temporary, caused by imports of capital goods that raise future output, and financed by FDI; it allows higher consumption and investment now.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: temporary/small; 1 mark: investment-led or sustainable financing [2]

items.stem: During a class discussion Diego said: ‘A current account deficit in Istrana will cause its currency to appreciate.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: A deficit means more of the currency is supplied (to buy imports) than demanded, putting downward pressure on its value.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A deficit means more of the currency is supplied (to buy imports) than demanded, putting downward pressure on its value. [2]

items.stem: Korvia has GDP of $500bn and runs a current account deficit of 6% of GDP each year, financed entirely by foreign borrowing. Calculate the annual deficit.
items.answer: $30bn

items.stem: For each case, identify the consequence of the current account imbalance and explain it. (i) Nordavia finances its large current account deficit by borrowing heavily from abroad. (ii) A persistent deficit leads to a fall in demand for Nordavia’s currency. (iii) Imports replace domestic output and factories close in Nordavia.
items.answer: (i) Rising foreign debt (ii) Pressure for depreciation (iii) Lower output and employment
items.markingKey: (i) Rising foreign debt – future interest payments increase primary income debits. [2] (ii) Pressure for depreciation – more currency is supplied to buy imports than is demanded for exports. [2] (iii) Lower output and employment – net exports are a leakage from aggregate demand. [2] Total [6]

items.stem: Which is included in secondary income in the current account?
options: Remittances sent home by migrant workers
Profits sent home by foreign firms
items.answer: Remittances sent home by migrant workers
items.markingKey: Current transfers.

items.stem: Explain why a country with a deficit on trade in goods can still have a current account surplus.
items.answer: Surpluses on trade in services, primary income or secondary income (e.g. tourism, financial services, investment income, remittances) can outweigh the goods deficit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: other components; 1 mark: example of a surplus offsetting the goods deficit [2]

items.stem: During a class discussion Aisha said: ‘The current account balance is exports of goods minus imports of goods.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: That is the trade in goods balance; the current account also includes services, primary income and secondary income.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – That is the trade in goods balance; the current account also includes services, primary income and secondary income. [2]

items.stem: A car maker in Sundara sells vehicles to buyers in Umbria Nova. Where, and on which side, is this transaction recorded in the current account of Sundara?
items.answer: Trade in goods (credit)
items.markingKey: Trade in goods (credit): export of goods brings money into Sundara.

items.stem: The table shows data for Kestria’s current account in one year. Exports of goods $180bn; imports of goods $280bn; exports of services $80bn; imports of services $45bn; primary income balance −$25bn; secondary income balance $8bn. (a) Calculate the balance of trade in goods and the balance of trade in services. (b) Calculate the current account balance.
items.answer: (a)/(b) Goods balance −$100bn; services balance $35bn; current account = −$100bn + $35bn + −$25bn + $8bn = −$82bn.
items.markingKey: (a) both balances [2] (b) [1] [3]

items.stem: Extract: Sundara’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 180, imports of goods 260, exports of services 60, imports of services 70, primary income balance −20, secondary income balance 15. GDP is $1200bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Calculate the current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP. (b) Explain why the primary income balance is negative.
items.answer: (a) −$95bn; −7.9% of GDP. (b) Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: −$95bn; −7.9% of GDP. [2] (b) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2]

items.stem: How might an appreciation of a country’s currency affect its current account?
options: It may worsen it, because exports become dearer and imports cheaper
items.answer: It may worsen it, because exports become dearer and imports cheaper
items.markingKey: Price competitiveness falls.

items.stem: In a revision note Ana wrote: ‘An appreciation of Dravonia’s currency will increase its exports.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: Appreciation raises the foreign-currency price of exports, so export volumes tend to fall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Appreciation raises the foreign-currency price of exports, so export volumes tend to fall. [2]

items.stem: A student, Diego, claims: ‘A current account deficit is always caused by uncompetitive firms.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: It may be cyclical (rapid growth in income and imports), or caused by an appreciation, high inflation or weak foreign demand, not only structural weakness.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – It may be cyclical (rapid growth in income and imports), or caused by an appreciation, high inflation or weak foreign demand, not only structural weakness. [2]

items.stem: Kestria has a marginal propensity to import of 0.3. Its national income rises by $20bn. Calculate the increase in imports.
items.answer: $6bn

items.stem: A recession in Ostrelia, Jovania’s main export market, reduces demand for Jovania’s exports. Which cause of a current account imbalance is described?
items.answer: Weak foreign demand (recession abroad)
items.markingKey: Weak foreign demand (recession abroad): lower foreign incomes reduce export demand.

items.stem: Calvania has a marginal propensity to import of 0.2. Its national income rises by $20bn. Calculate the increase in imports.
items.answer: $4bn

items.stem: Extract: Calvania’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 210, imports of goods 290, exports of services 60, imports of services 50, primary income balance −12, secondary income balance 15. GDP is $1000bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Calculate the current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP. (b) Explain why the primary income balance is negative.
items.answer: (a) −$67bn; −6.7% of GDP. (b) Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: −$67bn; −6.7% of GDP. [2] (b) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Rovania’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 240, imports of goods 320, exports of services 95, imports of services 40, primary income balance −20, secondary income balance 22. GDP is $1200bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Calculate the current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP. (b) Identify which component of the current account includes remittances. (c) Explain why the primary income balance is negative.
items.answer: (a) −$23bn; −1.9% of GDP. (b) Secondary income (current transfers). (c) Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: −$23bn; −1.9% of GDP. [2] (b) Credit: Secondary income (current transfers). [1] (c) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2]

items.stem: Why might a current account deficit reduce aggregate demand?
options: Exports are a leakage from the circular flow
Net exports (X − M) are a component of aggregate demand
items.answer: Net exports (X − M) are a component of aggregate demand
items.markingKey: Imports are a leakage.

items.stem: Pelora has a current account deficit of 7% of GDP, financed mainly by short-term bank loans. Explain why investors may become concerned.
items.answer: A large deficit financed by short-term loans is vulnerable: lenders may refuse to roll over loans, capital may flee, the currency may fall sharply and debt repayments rise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: size/short-term finance; 1 mark: risk of capital flight/depreciation [2]

items.stem: Kenji wrote in a homework answer: ‘A current account deficit always means that Istrana is poorer.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: A deficit means spending abroad exceeds earnings; it can reflect high consumption or investment financed by capital inflows and is not necessarily harmful if small and sustainable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A deficit means spending abroad exceeds earnings; it can reflect high consumption or investment financed by capital inflows and is not necessarily harmful if small and sustainable. [2]

items.stem: Loristan’s large surplus causes its currency to appreciate and trading partners to complain. Which consequence of a current account imbalance is described?
options: Pressure for appreciation and international tension
items.answer: Pressure for appreciation and international tension
items.markingKey: Pressure for appreciation and international tension: surpluses mean deficits elsewhere and demand for the currency.

items.stem: Pelora has GDP of $200bn and runs a current account deficit of 4% of GDP each year, financed entirely by foreign borrowing. GDP stays constant. The interest rate on the borrowing is 3% a year. (a) Calculate the total foreign debt after 10 years. (b) Calculate the annual interest payment on this debt.
items.answer: (a) Annual deficit = $8bn; after 10 years foreign debt = $80bn (40% of GDP). (b) Annual interest = 3% × $80bn = $2.4bn, 1.2% of GDP.

items.stem: Extract: Marvona’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 180, imports of goods 320, exports of services 60, imports of services 70, primary income balance −12, secondary income balance 10. GDP is $1000bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Explain two possible causes of the deficit on trade in goods. (b) Explain why the primary income balance is negative.
items.answer: (a) Strong credit-fuelled consumer demand raises imports (cyclical); the 8% appreciation makes exports dearer and imports cheaper. (b) Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Strong credit-fuelled consumer demand raises imports (cyclical); the 8% appreciation makes exports dearer and imports cheaper. [4] (b) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2]

items.stem: Spending by foreign tourists in a country is recorded as
options: a credit in trade in services
a credit in the financial account
a debit in trade in goods
items.answer: a credit in trade in services
items.markingKey: Tourism is an export of services.

items.stem: Isla makes the following statement: ‘Remittances sent home by migrant workers are recorded in primary income.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: Remittances are transfers with nothing given in return, so they are recorded in secondary income.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Remittances are transfers with nothing given in return, so they are recorded in secondary income. [2]

items.stem: Sipho wrote in a homework answer: ‘The current account balance is exports of goods minus imports of goods.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: That is the trade in goods balance; the current account also includes services, primary income and secondary income.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – That is the trade in goods balance; the current account also includes services, primary income and secondary income. [2]

items.stem: The table shows data for Halvoria’s current account in one year. Exports of goods $250bn; imports of goods $270bn; exports of services $75bn; imports of services $110bn; primary income balance −$8bn; secondary income balance $8bn. What is the current account balance?

The table shows data for Zentara’s current account in one year. Exports of goods $160bn; imports of goods $240bn; exports of services $35bn; imports of services $35bn; primary income balance −$4bn; secondary income balance $8bn. (a) Calculate the balance of trade in goods and the balance of trade in services. (b) Calculate the current account balance.
items.answer: (a)/(b) Goods balance −$80bn; services balance $0bn; current account = −$80bn + $0bn + −$4bn + $8bn = −$76bn.
items.markingKey: (a) both balances [2] (b) [1] [3]

Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Calculate the current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP. (b) Explain why the primary income balance is negative.

items.markingKey: (a) Credit: −$45bn; −4.5% of GDP. [2] (b) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2]

items.stem: Why might a country have a current account surplus?
options: Its domestic demand is growing very fast
Its exports are highly competitive and domestic saving is high
Its inflation rate is higher than its trading partners’
items.answer: Its exports are highly competitive and domestic saving is high
items.markingKey: Strong exports, low import demand.

items.stem: Dravonia has had a current account deficit in every year for 15 years, in booms and recessions. Explain what this suggests about the cause.
items.answer: A persistent deficit through the cycle suggests a structural cause, such as low productivity, poor quality or a narrow export base, rather than a cyclical one.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: structural; 1 mark: example of structural weakness [2]

items.stem: In a revision note Omar wrote: ‘An appreciation of Westaria’s currency will increase its exports.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Appreciation raises the foreign-currency price of exports, so export volumes tend to fall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Appreciation raises the foreign-currency price of exports, so export volumes tend to fall. [2]

items.answer: Weak foreign demand (recession abroad)
items.markingKey: Weak foreign demand (recession abroad): lower foreign incomes reduce export demand.

items.answer: $8bn

items.answer: Structural cause (lack of competitiveness)
items.markingKey: Structural cause (lack of competitiveness): long-term weakness in non-price and price competitiveness.

Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Calculate the current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP. (b) Explain why the primary income balance is negative.

items.markingKey: (a) Credit: −$78bn; −9.8% of GDP. [2] (b) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2]

GDP is $1200bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Calculate the current account balance and express it as a percentage of GDP. (b) Identify which component of the current account includes remittances. (c) Explain why the primary income balance is negative.
items.answer: (a) −$3bn; −0.2% of GDP. (b) Secondary income (current transfers). (c) Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: −$3bn; −0.2% of GDP. [2] (b) Credit: Secondary income (current transfers). [1] (c) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2]

items.stem: How is a current account deficit usually financed?
options: By a surplus on the financial account, such as borrowing or foreign investment
items.answer: By a surplus on the financial account, such as borrowing or foreign investment
items.markingKey: The balance of payments balances overall.

items.stem: Samuel makes the following statement: ‘A current account deficit in Kestria will cause its currency to appreciate.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: A deficit means more of the currency is supplied (to buy imports) than demanded, putting downward pressure on its value.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A deficit means more of the currency is supplied (to buy imports) than demanded, putting downward pressure on its value. [2]

items.stem: Hana wrote in a homework answer: ‘A current account deficit always means that Marvona is poorer.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: A deficit means spending abroad exceeds earnings; it can reflect high consumption or investment financed by capital inflows and is not necessarily harmful if small and sustainable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A deficit means spending abroad exceeds earnings; it can reflect high consumption or investment financed by capital inflows and is not necessarily harmful if small and sustainable. [2]

items.stem: Korvia has GDP of $500bn and runs a current account deficit of 4% of GDP each year, financed entirely by foreign borrowing. Calculate the annual deficit.
items.answer: $20bn

items.stem: Zentara has GDP of $500bn and runs a current account deficit of 8% of GDP each year, financed entirely by foreign borrowing. GDP stays constant. The interest rate on the borrowing is 6% a year. (a) Calculate the total foreign debt after 4 years. (b) Calculate the annual interest payment on this debt.
items.answer: (a) Annual deficit = $40bn; after 4 years foreign debt = $160bn (32% of GDP). (b) Annual interest = 6% × $160bn = $9.6bn, 1.92% of GDP.

items.stem: Extract: Istrana’s current account, latest year ($bn): exports of goods 240, imports of goods 320, exports of services 80, imports of services 70, primary income balance −8, secondary income balance 15. GDP is $1200bn. Consumer spending has been rising strongly, financed by credit, and the currency appreciated by 8% last year. Remittances from citizens working abroad are rising. Foreign investors hold a large share of government bonds. (a) Explain two possible causes of the deficit on trade in goods. (b) Explain why the primary income balance is negative.
items.answer: (a) Strong credit-fuelled consumer demand raises imports (cyclical); the 8% appreciation makes exports dearer and imports cheaper. (b) Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Strong credit-fuelled consumer demand raises imports (cyclical); the 8% appreciation makes exports dearer and imports cheaper. [4] (b) Credit: Interest on government bonds and profits paid to foreign investors exceed investment income received. [2]
